title: DataLoader Problems (Deadlock, Hanging, Slow Loading, Worker Crashes)
description: Troubleshooting and resolving PyTorch DataLoader failures, including worker deadlocks, hanging execution, slow data loading, and worker process crashes.
name: DataLoader Problems (Deadlock, Hanging, Slow Loading, Worker Crashes)

quick_identification.check: Training loop hangs at batch iteration
quick_identification.description: next(iter(dataloader)) or for batch in dataloader never returns.

quick_identification.check: Worker processes crash with signal errors
quick_identification.description: RuntimeError: DataLoader worker (pid X) is killed by signal: Killed or SIGSEGV.
Time next(dataloader_iter) and compare to compute step time.
nvidia-smi dmon shows GPU-Util cycling between high and idle states while workers fetch data.

symptoms.description: Training freezes indefinitely at data loading with no forward progress and no explicit exception.
symptoms.error_message: No explicit error; the process appears stuck.

symptoms.description: Worker processes terminate with segmentation fault or bus error.
symptoms.error_message: RuntimeError: DataLoader worker (pid X) is killed by signal: Segmentation fault or Bus error.
symptoms.where_appears: Worker spawn, batch collation, shared memory access.

symptoms.description: The OS OOM killer terminates worker processes due to excessive memory consumption.
symptoms.error_message: RuntimeError: DataLoader worker (pid X) is killed by signal: Killed.
symptoms.where_appears: Worker processes with large per-worker memory footprint.

symptoms.description: Batches load slowly despite fast storage, and the GPU sits idle between steps.
symptoms.error_message: No explicit error; training throughput is far below the compute-bound baseline.
symptoms.where_appears: Data loading pipeline, storage I/O, preprocessing.

root_causes.explanation: Multi-worker DataLoader transfers batch data through shared memory, and container defaults can exhaust /dev/shm, causing hangs or worker kills.
recognition_clues: df -h /dev/shm shows near-100% usage.
The issue appears only inside Docker or Kubernetes.
Increasing num_workers makes the problem worse.
The hang occurs at collation or worker transfer, not in __getitem__.
root_causes.typical_environment: Docker containers, Kubernetes pods, CI runners.

root_causes.explanation: Forking after CUDA initialization, open file handles, or lock creation can deadlock or corrupt child workers; PyTorch documents platform-specific start-method behavior and recommends careful multiprocessing design.
recognition_clues: The issue occurs only with num_workers > 0.
Switching to spawn or forkserver resolves it.
Dataset construction opens files, creates CUDA tensors, or initializes thread pools.
Worker logs mention CUDA initialization or serialization failures.
root_causes.typical_environment: Custom datasets with initialization side effects, GPU preprocessing, Linux multiprocessing workflows.

root_causes.cause: Excessive num_workers Relative to CPU or Memory
root_causes.explanation: Too many workers increase context switching, memory replication, and I/O contention; PyTorch warns that worker processes can consume as much CPU memory as the parent process for Python objects they access.
recognition_clues: htop shows all CPUs saturated and memory pressure rising with worker count.
Throughput improves at first, then plateaus or regresses as workers increase.
Swap usage or RSS growth tracks worker count.
root_causes.typical_environment: CPU-constrained instances, memory-limited containers, expensive preprocessing pipelines.

root_causes.explanation: High-latency storage such as NFS, EFS, or S3-backed mounts throttles random reads across workers, making the input pipeline I/O-bound.
recognition_clues: iostat -x 1 shows high await or near-saturated device utilization.
Copying data to local SSD removes the issue.
Worker traces spend time in read() or filesystem calls.
root_causes.typical_environment: Cloud NFS, object-storage mounts, HPC shared filesystems.

root_causes.explanation: Worker processes need serialized dataset and callback objects; lambdas, closures, open handles, or unpicklable third-party objects fail when workers are spawned.
recognition_clues: AttributeError: Can't pickle local object or TypeError: cannot pickle.
num_workers=0 works, but num_workers>0 fails immediately.
Failure occurs during worker startup rather than sample fetching.
root_causes.typical_environment: Custom datasets, inline transforms, notebook-defined functions.

root_causes.explanation: Locks, database connections, or nested parallelism inside dataset or collation code can deadlock when multiple workers contend.
recognition_clues: Hang occurs at the same batch index or data pattern.
Profilers show workers blocked on acquire or futex.
num_workers=0 works but multi-worker loading hangs.
root_causes.typical_environment: On-the-fly database access, locking augmentations, custom batch assembly.

root_causes.explanation: In DDP, uneven dataset lengths or uneven per-rank work can create stragglers that stall collective synchronization and trigger timeouts.
recognition_clues: NCCL timeout or elastic-agent worker death.
Some ranks finish early while others still iterate.
drop_last=False or imperfect sharding produces rank imbalance.
root_causes.typical_environment: Distributed training with custom sharding or uneven sample counts.

investigation_checklist.description: Run df -h /dev/shm to verify shared memory availability.
Verify the multiprocessing start method and prefer safer methods when fork-safety is questionable.

investigation_checklist.check: Check num_workers versus CPU core count
investigation_checklist.description: Verify num_workers does not exceed the host’s practical CPU budget.
Use iostat or a read benchmark to measure bandwidth and tail latency.
Test pickle.dumps(dataset) or equivalent serialization of worker inputs.

investigation_checklist.check: Check for CUDA context in dataset
investigation_checklist.description: Verify no CUDA calls occur in dataset initialization or sample retrieval.
Verify ranks see comparable sample counts and epoch boundaries.

diagnostic_commands.expected_output: Available space comfortably exceeds per-worker batch buffering needs.
diagnostic_commands.interpretation: Near-zero available space indicates shared memory exhaustion.

diagnostic_commands.command: ps aux | grep "DataLoader worker" | grep -v grep && top -b -n1 | grep "python"
diagnostic_commands.expected_output: Active worker processes with moderate CPU and memory usage.
diagnostic_commands.interpretation: Missing processes indicate crashes; high CPU wait suggests I/O bottlenecks.

diagnostic_commands.command: python -c "import time; t0 = time.time(); batch = next(iter(dataloader)); print(f'Batch load time: {time.time()-t0:.2f}s')"
diagnostic_commands.expected_output: Sub-second for light pipelines, and only a few seconds for heavy preprocessing.
diagnostic_commands.interpretation: Sustained >10s latency indicates storage or preprocessing bottlenecks.

diagnostic_commands.purpose: Check for pickling and fork-safety issues
diagnostic_commands.interpretation: PicklingError indicates non-serializable dataset state; CUDA-related failures point to fork-safety violations.

diagnostic_tests.test: Run the same job with larger container shared memory and compare behavior.
diagnostic_tests.expected_result: Hang or crash disappears with increased shared memory.
diagnostic_tests.interpretation: If fixed, /dev/shm exhaustion was the cause.
diagnostic_tests.next_action: Increase container shm allocation or mount host /dev/shm.

diagnostic_tests.test: Determine whether fork-safety violations are causing hangs or crashes.
diagnostic_tests.command: python -c "import torch.multiprocessing as mp; mp.set_start_method('spawn'); dl = DataLoader(ds, num_workers=4); next(iter(dl))"
diagnostic_tests.expected_result: Workers spawn successfully without CUDA or pickling errors.
diagnostic_tests.interpretation: If fixed, fork-safety was the issue.
diagnostic_tests.next_action: Refactor dataset to be fork-safe or use spawn permanently.

diagnostic_tests.test: Find the worker count that maximizes throughput without oversubscription.
diagnostic_tests.command: for n in 0 2 4 8 16; do python benchmark.py --num_workers=$n; done
diagnostic_tests.interpretation: The peak identifies the practical worker budget; regression at higher counts indicates oversubscription.
diagnostic_tests.next_action: Set num_workers to the best observed value, then re-benchmark after preprocessing changes.

decision_tree.question: Does the hang or crash occur only with num_workers > 0?

no.question: Does it occur with num_workers=0 too?

yes.result: The issue is in __getitem__ or storage; profile sample retrieval and I/O latency.

no.result: Intermittent race condition; inspect for locks or shared mutable state.

yes.question: Is this running inside a container?
Does df -h /dev/shm show low available space?

yes.result: Shared memory exhaustion; increase container shm or use a memory-backed mount.

no.question: Does switching to spawn fix it?

yes.result: Fork-safety violation; refactor dataset or keep spawn.

no.result: Check worker count oversubscription or storage I/O bottlenecks.

yes.result: Non-picklable dataset; remove lambdas, closures, or unpicklable objects.

no.question: Does htop show CPU saturation with high I/O wait?

yes.result: Storage bottleneck; cache data locally or reduce preprocessing.

no.question: Are you using DDP with uneven dataset lengths?

yes.result: Distributed straggler; use balanced sharding and appropriate sampler settings.

no.result: Custom deadlock in collate_fn or __getitem__; inspect with a profiler for lock contention.

solutions.quick_fix: Add --shm-size=8g to the Docker run command.
solutions.permanent_fix: Mount host /dev/shm or use a tmpfs-backed memory volume in Kubernetes.
steps: Check current usage: df -h /dev/shm.
Estimate required capacity from batch size, worker count, and sample size.
Increase shm allocation in Docker or Kubernetes.
Re-run the pipeline and confirm stable worker behavior.
Verify that /dev/shm headroom remains under peak throughput.
tradeoffs: Consumes host RAM and can compete with training memory.
Memory-backed volumes are constrained by pod or node limits.
solutions.performance_impact: Eliminates shm-related hangs; no inherent training slowdown.
solutions.verification: Training proceeds without worker crashes or deadlocks.

solutions.permanent_fix: Restructure the dataset so initialization is fork-safe and fully serializable.
steps: Call set_start_method('spawn', force=True) before any worker creation.
Move file opens out of __init__ and into lazy code paths.
Remove CUDA calls from dataset code.
Validate serialization with pickle.dumps(dataset).
Keep __main__-guarded entry points so worker import does not rerun setup code.
solutions.performance_impact: Slightly slower startup, but usually stable steady-state throughput.
works_for: Datasets with open file descriptors in initialization.
Linux workflows that otherwise rely on fork.
solutions.verification: Workers spawn without CUDA initialization or serialization failures.

solutions.quick_fix: Start with num_workers = cpu_count() // 2 and pin_memory = True for GPU training.
solutions.permanent_fix: Benchmark and standardize on a worker count that matches CPU, RAM, and preprocessing cost.
steps: Benchmark several worker counts.
Select the point where throughput stops improving.
Keep pin_memory=True when the output goes to CUDA devices.
Use persistent_workers=True for repeated epochs when worker startup is expensive.
Re-evaluate after preprocessing or storage changes.
tradeoffs: Too many workers increase context switching and memory pressure.
Persistent workers increase baseline memory use.
solutions.performance_impact: Often improves throughput substantially when the initial setting is suboptimal.
works_for: GPU training with host-to-device transfer bottlenecks.
solutions.verification: GPU utilization stays high and batch latency stays below compute time.

solutions.quick_fix: Copy datasets to local SSD before training starts.
solutions.permanent_fix: Add a staging layer that prefetches hot shards to local storage.
steps: Confirm the bottleneck with iostat or a simple read benchmark.
Sync data to local NVMe or equivalent local disk.
Point the dataset path to the local copy.
For very large datasets, prefetch the next shard in the background.
Re-measure end-to-end throughput.
tradeoffs: Adds job startup time for staging.
solutions.performance_impact: Can dramatically improve I/O-bound pipelines when network storage is the limit.
works_for: NFS, EFS, Filestore, and object-storage mounts.
solutions.verification: iostat shows lower latency and throughput approaches local-disk baseline.

solutions.solution: Fix Picklability and Remove CUDA from Dataset
solutions.quick_fix: Remove lambdas, nested functions, and CUDA tensors from dataset state.
solutions.permanent_fix: Keep dataset __init__ minimal and serializable, with only safe Python objects.
steps: Replace lambda transforms with module-level callables.
Move CUDA operations to the training loop.
Avoid storing unpicklable library objects in dataset state.
Re-test with pickle.dumps(dataset).
If needed, implement custom __getstate__ and __setstate__.
tradeoffs: Some third-party objects are not safe to serialize.
solutions.performance_impact: Usually neutral; may slightly increase code complexity.
solutions.verification: pickle.dumps(dataset) succeeds and workers start normally.

verification_checklist.description: for batch in dataloader runs to completion.
No crashes or OOM kills during a full epoch.
GPU idle time no longer dominates the training step.

verification_checklist.check: Batch loading latency is within budget
verification_checklist.description: Input pipeline time stays below compute time per step.

verification_checklist.check: Training throughput matches the expected maximum
verification_checklist.description: Samples per second is close to the compute-bound baseline.

practices: Test datasets with num_workers > 0 before scaling to full training.
Keep dataset initialization minimal and serializable; defer I/O to worker-side paths.
Profile data loading independently from model training.
Use persistent_workers=True and prefetch_factor=2 where repeated epochs justify the memory cost.
Provision enough shared memory for multi-worker loading in containers.
Treat num_workers as a tuned parameter, not a constant default.
Stage remote datasets to local disk when I/O latency dominates.
Set distributed timeout policies that reflect expected data-staging latency.
Track worker crash rates and restart counts.
Never call CUDA from dataset code.
Avoid lambdas and closures in dataset transforms.
Implement __getstate__ and __setstate__ for datasets with non-picklable state.
Keep custom collate_fn implementations free of hidden locks and blocking I/O.

common_misconceptions.reality: Throughput eventually regresses due to context switching, memory contention, and I/O saturation.
Problems usually arise when pinned-memory loading combines with insufficient shared memory in containers.

common_misconceptions.misconception: fork is always faster and therefore always better
common_misconceptions.reality: fork starts quickly but is fragile with CUDA and thread-using code; safer start methods can be the right tradeoff.

false_positive_cases.why_it_looks_similar: The job appears to hang during loading.
false_positive_cases.how_to_distinguish: Code explicitly waits on barriers or sleeps; GPU idle time is expected.

false_positive_cases.why_it_looks_similar: The first batch takes much longer than later batches.
false_positive_cases.how_to_distinguish: The delay is in model execution, not the data pipeline.
Latency correlates with sequence length or sample complexity, not worker failure.

escalation_paths.path: Implement custom data loading with Ray or DALI
escalation_paths.when_to_use: PyTorch DataLoader cannot meet throughput requirements.

escalation_paths.path: Use WebDataset or IterableDataset for streaming
escalation_paths.when_to_use: The dataset is too large for local staging.
Preprocessing is the dominant bottleneck and can be amortized.
